name: Arb (archived original repository)
baseline: mpmath 0.19 (also Mathematica 9.0 for the table; README also says about as fast as MPFR and about twice as fast as MPFI)
workload: Time in seconds to evaluate the Gauss hypergeometric function 2F1(1/2, 1/4, 1, z) at z = sqrt(5) + sqrt(7)i to 10, 100, 1000 and 10000 decimal digits (arbitrary-precision special function evaluation with rigorous error bounds).
claimed_speedup: README table (seconds, Mathematica 9.0 / mpmath 0.19 / Arb 2.8-git): 10 digits 0.00066 / 0.00065 / 0.000071; 100 digits 0.0039 / 0.0012 / 0.00048; 1000 digits 0.23 / 1.2 / 0.0093; 10000 digits 42.6 / 84 / 0.56. Ratios vs mpmath (derived from page data): about 9.2x at 10 digits, 2.5x at 100, 129x at 1000, 150x at 10000; vs Mathematica about 9.3x, 8.1x, 25x, 76x. README prose: 'For basic arithmetic, Arb should generally be around as fast as MPFR, though it can be a bit slower at low precision, and around twice as fast as MPFI' and transcendental functions 'should generally be faster than any other arbitrary-precision software currently available'.
hardware: 1.90 GHz Intel i5-4300U (Arb and mpmath); 3.07 GHz Intel Xeon X5675 (Mathematica 9.0)
stars_or_usage: 483 stars (archived original; development continues inside FLINT)
tradeoffs: Midpoint-radius ball arithmetic: every result carries a rigorous error bound, which costs some overhead against plain floating point (README: can be a bit slower than MPFR at low precision). Depends on FLINT and GMP or MPIR. LGPL-2.1-or-later. The repo is archived; use FLINT for current code.
caveats: SAME PROJECT AS https://github.com/flintlib/arb, which the catalog already holds (merged.json, tier B, baseline MPFR dot product from arXiv 1901.04289); this record is the archived original repo with a different benchmark (README 2F1 table), so fold it into that entry with decision duplicate or use it as extra evidence. README table only: single hypergeometric function, single point, one run per cell; mpmath 0.19 is an old pure-Python release (whether gmpy was installed is not stated), Mathematica 9.0 ran on a different, faster-clocked CPU than Arb and mpmath; no benchmark script or compiler flags in the repo (top level has module directories, doc and examples only), so tier C rather than A. The README says Arb 2.8-git (circa 2016). The peer-reviewed Arb paper (Johansson, 'Arb: Efficient Arbitrary-Precision Midpoint-Radius Interval Arithmetic', arXiv 1611.02831, ARITH 2017) has Table 2 comparing Arb with MPFR 3.1.5 and MPFI 1.5.1 on an i5-4300U (per a search-result snippet only: Arb ratios to MPFR roughly 1.0-1.8 for add, mul and div, MPFI roughly 2.0-3.0); arxiv.org, hal and fredrikj.net are egress-blocked here, so I could not open it and no number from it is used in claimed_speedup. A paper-access retier could lift this to B. No comparison against GMP (the suggested baseline) exists because GMP has no interval or special-function layer.

name: Box2D (v3.2 development, main branch)
baseline: Box2D v3.1.1 (previous release of the same library)
workload: Whole-scene simulation step time (ms, lower is better) on the 14 benchmark scenes in shared/benchmarks.c (compounds, joint_grid, junkyard, large_pyramid, many_pyramids, rain, smash, spinner, tumbler, washer, queries, tree_cast, tile_world, sleep) at 60 Hz with 4 substeps, 1 thread and 8 threads, all steps after the first, world creation excluded.
claimed_speedup: benchmark/performance_v320.md: 'Box2D v3.2 steps the same scenes about twice as fast as v3.1.1'; geometric mean 2.04x on one thread and 2.19x on eight threads (headline 2.0x and 2.2x) across 14 scenes. Examples (v3.1.1 to v3.2, ms): large_pyramid 1 thread 2070 to 727 (2.85x), 8 threads 370 to 137 (2.70x); many_pyramids 3095 to 1047 (2.96x), 458 to 151 (3.03x); sleep 4592 to 1454 (3.16x), 744 to 247 (3.01x); junkyard 5918 to 2038 (2.90x). Smallest gains: queries 1655 to 1286 (1.29x), tree_cast 1203 to 917 (1.31x), joint_grid 2613 to 1969 (1.33x). SSE2-forced v3.2 alone gives 1.83x (1 thread) and 2.03x (8 threads); AVX2 runtime dispatch adds about 10%.
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 19.51, Release, default CMake options for each version; AVX2 kernels chosen at runtime; turbo disabled via power plan (processor state pinned at 99%)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D, Windows 11; threads pinned to one hardware thread on each of eight cores (start /affinity 0x5555); each value is the minimum of four runs in two interleaved rounds, spread under 4% in nearly every cell
tradeoffs: 2D only, portable C17 with a C API; v3 is a rewrite whose behaviour differs from v2.4 (see docs/migration.md); world is not thread-safe for writes (read-only queries may be called from several threads); multithreading uses the built-in task scheduler via b2WorldDef::workerCount; AVX2 and SSE2/Neon kernels selected at runtime.
caveats: SELF-COMPARISON: the baseline is the project's own previous release, not another engine. Box2D is 2D only, so ODE and Bullet (the guessed baselines, both 3D) are not comparable and the repo contains no comparison against any other engine. v3.2 is unreleased (latest GitHub release is v3.1.1; the numbers come from the main branch, file touched by commit ac7c751 on 2026-10-04). The page says 'These are relative numbers from one machine. Read the ratios, not the milliseconds.' v3.1.1 ran the v3.2 scenes after they were 'ported to the v3.1.1 API without changing them' (port not published in that file); v3.1.1 used enkiTS for threading while v3.2 uses its built-in scheduler; and v3.2 creates fewer contacts because of a tighter broad-phase AABB margin (washer 29k vs 42k contacts), so the work per step is not identical (the page counts that as an engine improvement). The benchmark folder also holds per-machine CSVs (amd7950x_avx2, amd7950x_sse2, amd7950x_float, m2air_float, m2air_neon, n100_sse2) that I listed but did not open. Independent but weak extra evidence (not used for the tier): the third-party repo Ughuuu/benchmarks-repo (docs/REPORT-2D.md, Godot 4.7, 300 timed steps, single run, no CPU model stated, macOS arm64 builds) measures Box2D v3 through the godot-box2d-v3 addon against GodotPhysics2D and Rapier2D: pyramid 24.06 ms vs 151.83 ms (GodotPhysics2D) and 19.47 ms (Rapier2D wins); mixed_pile 5.91 ms vs 64.78 ms and 8.77 ms; joint_grid 3.83 ms vs 7.99 ms (Rapier2D) but Box2D's displacement_max is reported as inf; smash 11.52 ms vs 12.42 ms (Rapier2D) and 50.63 ms; query_storm 4.28 ms vs 7.11 ms and 63.39 ms; drop 21.10 ms vs 17.81 ms (Rapier2D wins). That run includes Godot addon overhead and is not a clean engine comparison.

name: Bullet Physics (bullet3)
workload: Gazebo-classic free-floating rigid boxes benchmark (1x4x9 boxes tumbling, 1 to 101 boxes in steps of 20, collision flag 0 and 1): ratio of wall-clock time to simulated time (timeRatio, lower is faster) for 10 s simulated at a 0.0005 s step (Simbody at 0.001 s), engine selected inside Gazebo-classic.
claimed_speedup: test_results/BENCHMARK_boxes_model_count.csv timeRatio, Bullet vs DART vs Simbody vs ODE: 101 boxes, collision flag 1: 1.4384 vs 7.22947 vs 1.87016 vs 1.3357; 101 boxes, flag 0: 1.47622 vs 4.37142 vs 1.84033 vs 1.58186; 81 boxes, flag 0: 1.1899 vs 3.1365 vs 1.48602 vs 1.23362; 1 box, flag 0: 0.127279 vs 0.136993 vs 0.12391 vs 0.101879. Derived from page data: Bullet about 5.0x faster than DART (101 boxes, flag 1), 3.0x (flag 0), 1.30x and 1.25x faster than Simbody at the same counts; Bullet faster than DART and Simbody in all 12 configurations; Bullet about 1.07x faster than ODE at 101 and 81 boxes with flag 0 but slower than ODE in the other 10 of 12 configurations (for example 101 boxes, flag 1: ODE 1.3357 vs Bullet 1.4384, about 1.08x). ROSCon 2014 slides, Benchmark 3 object stacking (time ratio real/sim): ODE 0.4, Bullet 0.5, DART 1.1, Simbody >100.
stars_or_usage: 14.8k stars; used in games, VFX, robotics (PyBullet) and Gazebo
tradeoffs: Maximal-coordinate rigid-body solver with impulse contacts and explicit joint damping (ROSCon 2014 slide), so stiff articulated robots need small steps; broad feature set (soft bodies, vehicles, PyBullet bindings). The GitHub issue tracker is closed to support questions (README).
caveats: Numbers are from a third-party Gazebo-classic benchmark (OSRF engineers; repo scpeters/benchmark, Apache-2.0, 16 stars) that I downloaded as a CSV and the ROSCon 2014 slides (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scpeters/benchmark/HEAD/pdf/roscon2014_scpeters.pdf), roughly 2014-2015 vintage. No CPU model, compiler or flags, and no Bullet or DART version are stated, and Bullet runs through Gazebo-classic's plugin so Gazebo overhead is included; hence tier C. The headline wins are over DART and Simbody, not over ODE or a game-engine rival: ODE is faster than Bullet in 10 of 12 configurations, and Bullet wins only at 81 and 101 boxes with collision flag 0 by about 7%. DART's angular momentum error in the same CSV is 2.36521 against 0.00626 for Bullet, and Simbody runs at a 0.001 s step against 0.0005 s for the others, so the speed rows are not accuracy- or step-matched. The stacking slide labels its numbers 'Time ratio (real / sim)' without saying which direction is faster; lower is faster by that definition and Simbody's '>100' fits a slow engine. Same benchmark source as the ODE entry already in the catalog. The repo README and docs carry no benchmark numbers of Bullet's own; no Bullet-vs-PhysX or Bullet-vs-Jolt numbers were reachable (per the catalog's existing Jolt Physics entry, a PlayCanvas PR shows Ammo.js, an Emscripten build of Bullet, level with or faster than Jolt while bodies collide; I did not open that PR). Last commit 2026-10-09 is README-only; the last code change I saw is 2025-10-22 (pyproject.toml).
